item.title: No Perfect Randomized Composition
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Alexander Meiburg

Does computing a composition of total Boolean functions require the product of the randomized query complexities of its factors? We give a negative answer. There are families of total functions $f,g$ such that $R(f\circ g) =Θ\!\left(\frac1{\log R(g)}\right)R(f)R(g)$ This result requires first separating linearized query complexity $\LR$, as well as noisy randomized query complexity $noisyR$, from standard randomized query complexity $R$. Both constructions essentially come from totalizing existing partial function separations, albeit via different techniques. By adapting these techniques, we also construct total functions separating every adjacent pair in the chain from sabotage $RS$, max-conflict $\barχ$, and linearised query complexity $LR$. We show that AND-of-ORs separates conflict $χ$ from max-conflict $\barχ$ complexity and makes conflict and sabotage incomparable. Finally, randomized complexity can be smaller than its composition limit $R^*$ by the maximal factor $Θ(\log R)$. The total--total composition separation is also formalized in Lean.

item.title:
TR26-269 | Settling Nondeterministic Communication Complexity of Graph Connectivity |
Zhijun Zhang
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Determining the communication complexity of graph connectivity has been one of the longest standing open problems in communication complexity since the seminal work of Babai, Frankl, and Simon [FOCS'86]. A simple protocol transmits a spanning forest using $O(N\log N)$ communication on $N$-vertex graphs. While this was shown optimal for deterministic protocols by Hajnal, Maass, and Turán [STOC'88], the optimal nondeterministic and randomized complexities have remained unresolved for decades. We settle the nondeterministic communication complexity of graph connectivity by proving an optimal $\Omega(N\log N)$ lower bound. The best prior bound was $\Omega(N\log\log N)$ due to Raz and Spieker [Combinatorica'95]. Our bound is shown by upper bounding the maximum size of $1$-monochromatic rectangles. Generalizing our techniques to weighted, almost $1$-monochromatic rectangles yields an $\Omega(N \cdot \log(\min(1/\varepsilon,N)))$ lower bound for randomized protocols with error probability $\varepsilon$. In particular, this bound is optimal for any polynomially small $\varepsilon$. For constant error probability, we also prove that any $r$-round protocol requires $\Omega(N/r \cdot \log N)$ communication, which is optimal for every constant $r$. Previously, optimal $\Omega(N\log N)$ lower bounds for graph connectivity were known only for $1$-round [Sun, Woodruff; APPROX/RANDOM'15] and $2$-round protocols [Radhakrishnan, Reddy, Venkat; ITCS'26]. Our proof introduces a new communication problem which can be viewed as a composition of inner product and pointer chasing problems. Our lower bounds can be extended to other fundamental graph properties, and also imply optimality of known query and streaming algorithms for related problems.

item.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Niels Inselmann Christiansen, Eva Rotenberg

We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in some biconnected graph G in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries of the form "are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between a and b?". All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. All queries and updates are answered in worst-case $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get an algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case running time of $O(\log^2 n)$ per operation. These algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.

item.title: A Nearly Optimal Min-Cut Algorithm for Dynamic Streams
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: dynamic stream

Authors: Yang P. Liu, Hoai-An Nguyen, Vihan Shah, David P. Woodruff

We give an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space algorithm for the minimum cut problem in dynamic streams, resolving the space complexity of streaming min-cut up to polylogarithmic factors. Ding, Garces, Li, Lin, Nelson, Shah, and Woodruff (ITCS 2025) obtained the same $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$ space bound for insertion-only streams, while prior to our work the best known bound even for unweighted dynamic streams was $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$, due to Ahn, Guha, and McGregor (PODS 2012). Our main technical contribution is an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space for-each cut sketch in dynamic streams, which may be of independent interest. The construction applies to weighted graphs under general $\pmΔ$ updates, a stronger model than the standard dynamic-stream setting in which weighted edges are inserted and deleted in their entirety. Despite this stronger guarantee, our algorithm is surprisingly simple and relies on very little machinery. We also obtain applications to minimum $\ell_p$-norm $k$-partitioning for every fixed $k$, weighted correlation-clustering evaluation for two clusters, and for-each cut sketching in balanced directed graphs.

item.title: When is greedy exact for weighted minimum 3-cut?
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Armando Rodado Amaris

The greedy algorithm for minimum 3-cut splits a global minimum-weight cut and then the cheaper of its two sides; it is a tight $4/3$-approximation. We show that it is exact, from every global minimum-weight cut, whenever some optimal 3-partition has two parts joined by total weight at least the weighted edge connectivity $λ$. This extends both theorems of Hochbaum and Shmoys from unweighted planar graphs to all weighted graphs, recovers the $4/3$ bound, and generalizes to minimum $k$-cut with a one-paragraph proof. The remaining hard instances have all pair weights below $λ$; for them we prove a merge lemma for Gomory-Hu sides. Finally, we give a 7-vertex graph with a unique Gomory-Hu tree whose unique optimal 3-partition contains no side of that tree, so the first stage of Kapoor's algorithm does not suffice on its own. The main theorem, the 4/3 bound, the merge lemmas and the counterexample are verified in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

item.title: Extrinsic Curvature Estimation by Closest Point Projection of Rays
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: neighbor query

Authors: Liangchen Liu, Yen-Hsi Richard Tsai

We propose a parametrization-free framework for estimating the second fundamental form and the principal curvatures of a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The method uses the closest point projections of a few short random rays and recovers the curvature from the curves that these projections induce on the submanifold, without coordinate charts or local fitting. We analyze the geometry of the induced curves and characterize when they are geodesics. For hypersurfaces, these results give two algorithms with error bounds: a least squares reconstruction of the second fundamental form from the curvatures of the induced curves, and a direct estimate of all principal curvatures from the eigenvalues of a $d\times d$ matrix built from $d$ rays, which needs no normal information and costs $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ besides the projections. In higher codimension, we can also recover the second fundamental form one normal direction at a time. On point clouds, where the projection becomes a nearest neighbor query, we bound the additional error. Experiments confirm the predicted rates for hypersurfaces in up to $128$ dimensions, for surfaces of codimension up to $98$, and on point clouds, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in practice.

item.title: Local-to-Global Theorems Based on Cones with Applications to Graph Coloring
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: graph coloring

Authors: Anqi Li, Shayan Oveis Gharan

Local-to-Global theorems are a cornerstone of many of recent developments in theoretical computer science from coding theory and PCPs all the way to analyzing mixing time of Markov chains. Building on trickledown theorems on simplicial complexes, several techniques have been established to obtain tighter local-to-global theorems to analyze the spectral gap of the Glauber dynamics, namely matrix trickledown, ${\mathcal C}$-Lorentzian polynomials and more recently Bochner type inequalities. In this paper, we adopt non-local local-to-global/Bochner type inequalities on "cones", corresponding to the local neighborhood of a given vertex, to show that the Glauber dynamics mixes in polynomial time to sample proper colorings of maximum degree $Δ$ graphs as long as $q\geq 1.7408Δ$.

item.title: An Unconditional Space-Approximation Lower Bound for Semi-Streaming Matching
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: semi-streaming

Authors: Yang P. Liu, Kheeran Naidu, Hoai-An Nguyen, Janani Sundaresan

We prove the first unconditional lower bound tradeoff between the number of passes and the approximation factor of maximum matchings in the semi-streaming model. Specifically, we show that any algorithm that outputs an $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation to maximum matching requires $Ω(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ passes for constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Prior to our result, such tradeoffs were proven only conditioned on a certain combinatorial assumption about the density of Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. The state-of-the-art unconditional lower bound rules out any approximation factor better than $(8/9)$ in two passes but leaves open the possibility of a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for any $\varepsilon > 0$ even in three passes. We provide two different proofs of our result: the first proof uses the recent hierarchical-embedding framework of Assadi, Konrad, Naidu, and Sundaresan (STOC 2024) along with combinatorial constructions using Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. The second extends the two-level Ruzsa-Szemerédi hierarchy of Konrad and Naidu (SODA 2024) beyond two levels and proves the corresponding communication lower bound directly by induction, rather than through a reduction to Index.

item.title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Majid Daliri, Mohammadreza Daneshvaramoli, Purna Dutta, Edo Liberty, Cameron Musco, Christopher Musco, Torsten Suel

Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.

item.title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part II: Langevin Dynamics
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Aniket Das, Tselil Schramm

We consider the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem on the sphere, in which we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\mathcal{S}_N=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\lVert x\rVert^2=N\}$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. Continuing the program initiated in Part I [arXiv:2610.16705], we show that spherical Langevin dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, our results demonstrate that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

item.title:
TR26-286 | On the complexities of Interactive Proofs of Proximity |
Noga Amit,
Oded Goldreich
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

The plural in the title hints that there are several complexities involved here. The most traditional one is the computational complexity of the verifier; but, in the context of Interactive Proofs of Proximity (IPPs), the query complexity of the verifier and the communication complexity of the system should take the front seat. Hence, we avoid limiting the computational complexity of the verifier, since this limitation blurs the role of the main complexity measures that should be of interest in the case of IPPs. Specifically, we consider IPPs in which the verifier strategy is only restricted by its query complexity and its communication complexity. While we do not limit the computational complexity of the verifier, we do care about the computational complexity of the properties for which we prove a query+communication lower bound. Our results present a trade-off between the computational complexity of the properties for which query+communication lower bounds are asserted and complexity assumptions that condition these results. Specifically, letting $q$ and $c$ denote the query and communication complexities of IPPs (and letting $n$ denote the input length), we essentially prove \begin{enumerate} \item An unconditional lower bound of $q(n)+c(n)=\Omega(n/\log n)$ for properties that are decidable in double-exponential time. \item Assuming that exponential-time (resp., NP) contains a set that does not have (non-uniform) small-exponential circuit size, we obtain a $q(n)+c(n)=\Omega(n/\log n)$ lower bound for properties that are decidable in exponential-time (resp., in NP). \item Assuming the existence of pseudorandom generators that fool small-exponential size circuits, we obtain a lower bound of $q(n)+c(n)=\Omega({\sqrt{n/\log n}})$ for properties that are decidable in P. \end{enumerate} In contrast, recall that any property in uniform-NC has an IPP with $q(n)+c(n)={\widetilde O}({\sqrt n})$. Hence, the almost linear lower bounds of the first two items are unlikely to be proven unconditionally for properties in NP. In the foregoing text, $c(n)$ denotes the total number of bits exchanged between the two parties (in both directions). One may wonder whether similar bounds hold when considering only the number of bits communicated by the prover, denoted $p(n)$. We show that this is essentially the case, by proving that the verifier gains almost nothing by sending messages of length exceeding $O(q(n)\cdot\log n)$. Specifically, we show that if $\Pi$ has an $r(n)$-round IPP in which the prover sends at most $p(n)$ bits and the verifier makes at most $q(n)$ queries, then $\Pi$ has an $r(n)$-round IPP of query complexity $O(q(n))$ and communication complexity $O(p(n)+r(n)\cdot q(n)\cdot\log n)$.

item.title: ExplainCC: Explaining Correlated Clusters by Node Labels
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: correlation clustering

Authors: Nadeesha Shyami Kumari Herath Mudiyanselage, Florian Adriaens, Nikolaj Tatti

An increasingly important requirement for clustering algorithms is that decisions and outcomes need to be clearly understandable for human users. We address this requirement for the Correlation Clustering (CC) problem, in case the objects to be clustered are accompanied by labels. In CC one seeks to partition a set of objects into clusters based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity information. Our proposed model only considers clusters that can be explained by a label tree, which is essentially a decision tree that partitions the objects according to labels. The goal is to find an explainable partition of the data that minimizes the CC objective function. We formalize this problem from a theoretical viewpoint, and prove several hardness of approximation results, also when constraining the size of the tree. Our proposed greedy method finds locally optimal splits, and works recursively in a top-down approach. To efficiently compute the best split, we carefully maintain certain counters. An experimental evaluation demonstrates its effectiveness. The proposed algorithm processes graphs with over million edges in a few minutes, can find the ground truth in synthetic data, and is able to produce interpretable clusters in real world networks.

item.title: Fully Dynamic All-Pairs Min Cuts on Planar Graphs via Planar Pattern Emulators
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: Arnold Filtser, Gramoz Goranci, Ali Momeni, Neel Patel, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg

We study the fully-dynamic all-pairs minimum cut problem on planar graphs. Given an $n$-vertex undirected planar graph $G=(V,E)$ undergoing edge insertions and deletions, the goal is to efficiently process these updates while supporting $s$-$t$ minimum cut queries for any pair of vertices $s$ and $t$. We give a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate dynamic algorithm that supports edge updates and minimum cut queries in $n^{o(1)}$ time, for any $1/\text{poly}(\log n) < \varepsilon < 1$. For general graphs, previous results either are limited to partially dynamic settings or achieve only logarithmic-factor approximations. The main conceptual and technical contribution is to show that a suitable adaptation of the planar emulator of Chang, Krauthgamer, and Tan~[STOC'22] satisfies the stronger pattern emulator introduced by Chen and Tan~[ICALP'25]. This leads almost immediately to a nearly linear-time construction of pattern emulators, which, when combined with the recent fully dynamic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate all-pairs shortest paths algorithm of Filtser, Goranci, Patel, and Probst Gutenberg~[FOCS'24], yields our result.

item.title: Dynamic $(Δ+1)$ Vertex Coloring with Adaptive Adversaries: Entropy Compression to the Rescue
item.description:
Filter match: person: sepehr assadi

Authors: Sepehr Assadi, Helia Yazdanyar

We present a randomized algorithm for maintaining a $(Δ+1)$ vertex coloring of a fully dynamic graph against an adaptive adversary with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ amortized update time. Our algorithm improves upon the recent randomized algorithms of Behnezhad, Rajaraman, and Wasim (SODA 2025) with $\tilde{O}(n^{8/9})$ and Flin and Halldórsson (ICALP 2025) with $\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})$ amortized update time. Our result (nearly) matches a fundamental limit of $O(\sqrt{n})$ update time identified by Flin and Halldórsson and settles their main open question. The previous algorithms' main improvement came from efficient coloring of the dense parts of the graph. Our approach complements these prior work by handling the sparse parts more efficiently, using ideas inspired by the recently developed dynamic entropy compression method. A key new aspect of our work is to tailor this method specifically to dynamic algorithms---as opposed to original local search algorithms---and achieve update times that can be sublinear in the number of involved constraints per update.

item.title: Fast Perfect $L_2$ Sampling
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: data stream

Authors: David P. Woodruff, Samson Zhou

Perfect $L_2$ sampling is a powerful primitive for turnstile data streams, allowing algorithms to extract an index with probability proportional to its squared frequency, with applications to dynamic join size estimation, query optimization, heavy-hitters, sampling from self-joins, and real-time monitoring of evolving datasets. The setting $p=2$ is also the largest $p$ for which $L_p$ sampling can be achieved in polylogarithmic space. However, existing space-optimal perfect samplers rely on explicit polynomial duplication, requiring inefficient polynomial update times per stream arrival. Resolving a open question left by Swartworth, Woodruff, and Zhou [FOCS 2025], we present a perfect $L_2$ sampler that achieves an expected $\text{polylog}(n)$ update time while maintaining an optimal $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log^3 n)$ bits of space.

item.title: Local Important Separators with Applications to Unbreakable Decomposition and Multicut
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Aditya Anand, Euiwoong Lee, Yaowei Long, Thatchaphol Saranurak

We present the first local FPT algorithm for finding important separators: Given an undirected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, vertices $s,t$ and parameters $k$ and $ν$, we can enumerate all $s$-$t$ important separators of size at most $k$ and volume at most $ν$ in time $\tilde{O}(ν2^{O(k)})$. Known approaches spend either $Ω(m)$ time (not local) or $ν^{Ω(k)}$ time (not FPT). Using this local algorithm, we show the following applications. (1) The first is an improved construction of unbreakable decomposition, a powerful generalization of tree decompositions. For any $k$, we can compute a $(5k,k)$-unbreakable decomposition with adhesion $4k$ in $\tilde{O}(k^{O(k)}m)$ time. This strictly subsumes the result of Anand, Lee, Li, Long, and Saranurak (SODA 2025) and is faster than the recent $O(k^{O(k^2)}m)$-time algorithm by Korhonen (STOC 2025) when $k = ω\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{\log \log n}{\log \log \log n}}\Bigr)$. Our algorithm is also simpler than that of Korhonen (STOC 2025). (2) We give a near-linear time algorithm for single-sink important separators. For any sink $t$, we can list all $v$-$t$ important separators of size at most $k$ across all $v \in V(G)$ in time $\tilde{O}(2^{O(k)}m)$. Known approaches trivially compute $v$-$t$ important separators for each $v$, taking $Ω(4^k k mn)$ time. (3) Using the above result on single-sink important separators, we speed up undirected shadow removal and give the first almost-linear time FPT algorithm for Edge Multicut.

item.title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: max-cut

Authors: Konstantin Kutzkov

We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-γ)n})$, for a fixed $γ>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.

item.title: Dimension Reduction and Coresets for Min-Sum $k$-Clustering
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Asaf Dallal, Robert Krauthgamer

The min-sum $k$-clustering problem asks to partition an input of $n$ points into $k$ clusters so as to minimize the total pairwise distance within clusters. It is a natural alternative to center-based objectives when the data is not well captured by a small set of representative points. We study for this problem two standard sketching methods, dimension reduction and coresets, which represent the input more compactly while preserving the min-sum cost of every $k$-partition up to $1\pm\varepsilon$ factor. Our first contribution addresses dimension reduction in Euclidean space. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) Lemma readily implies that a random linear map to target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ preserves, with high probability, the min-sum cost of all $k$-partitions. We show that target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}(ddim\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log k+\log\log n))$ suffices for Euclidean inputs of doubling dimension at most $ddim$, and moreover this bound is nearly optimal. We also show that target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log k+\logΔ))$ suffices for Euclidean inputs of aspect ratio at most $Δ$. Our second contribution is to design the first $\varepsilon$-coreset for metric min-sum $k$-clustering. It is actually a movement-based coreset, has size $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(ddim)} k\log n$ for inputs of doubling dimension at most $ddim$, and can be constructed in randomized near-linear-time. We further use these coresets to design streaming algorithms for the problem.

item.title: Upper Bounds for CSP Non-redundancy via Locally Decodable Codes
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Joshua Brakensiek, David Conlon, Venkatesan Guruswami, Xiaoyu He, Jiaxi Nie, Maya Sankar, Hung-Hsun Hans Yu

In the study of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), the non-redundancy of a relation measures the maximum number of clauses in a CSP instance which can be logically independent. In the last few years, CSP non-redundancy has found a number of applications including in query complexity, sparsification, kernelization and streaming. In this paper, we present a novel technique for upper-bounding the non-redundancy of some relations using locally decodable codes (LDCs) and locally correctable codes (LCCs). More precisely, known limitations on the structure of 2-query LDCs and LCCs can be translated into limitations on the size of certain non-redundant CSP instances. This technique builds on a technique used by Brakensiek and Guruswami [STOC 2025] to bound non-redundancy via techniques from matching vector codes. Using LDCs and LCCs, we give improved upper bounds on non-redundancy of the BCK predicate pioneered by Bessiere, Carbonnel, and Katsirelos [AAAI 2020] as well as its well-studied Boolean variant. We also give the first example of a Boolean predicate whose non-redundancy is provably not of the form $n^{k\pm o(1)}$ for some positive integer $k$.

item.title: Directed Cut-Query Complexity of Finding a King
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Ziad Ismaili Alaoui, Oded Lachish, Nikhil S. Mande

A king in a tournament is a vertex from which every other vertex is reachable by a directed path of length at most two. We study the deterministic query complexity of finding a king when a query specifies a set of vertices and returns the number of edges directed from that set to its complement. We prove that this complexity is $Θ(n)$ for $n$-vertex tournaments. To show this, we first show that every correct deterministic algorithm in this model must output a maximum-outdegree vertex, even though a king need not have maximum outdegree. We then give an adversary whose answers, after too few queries, remain consistent with a tournament in which the algorithm's output does not have maximum outdegree.

item.title: Galactus the Devourer
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post is about the history of failing to rigorously define efficiency in computer science. Like my previous post on Fourier transforms, it’s more technical than usual, but I tried to make it as accessible as possible.

I’ve always been fascinated by this pernicious pattern in the practice of applied mathematics, which I wrote about here a few weeks ago:

Applied mathematicians often need to build a giant scaffolding of mathematical modeling to solve a problem. This scaffolding creates new mathematical puzzles that aren’t directly connected to the original problem of interest, but that entice problem solvers. You’ll then see dozens of follow-up papers solving the puzzles but forgetting the problem we cared about in the first place.

There is probably no better example of such forgetting than the field of complexity theory.

In 1965, Jack Edmonds came up with a clever way to find a maximum matching in a graph. He wanted to argue that his algorithm could be computed “efficiently,” as the procedure was a bit complicated and required a computer to run. But he found he didn’t have the language to describe what it would mean for an algorithm to be efficient. In Section 2 of his paper, named “Digression,” he wrote,

According to the dictionary, “efficient” means “adequate in operation or performance.” This is roughly the meaning I want—in the sense that it is conceivable for maximum matching to have no efficient algorithm. Perhaps a better word is “good.”

I am claiming, as a mathematical result, the existence of a good algorithm.

Edmonds noted that he could enumerate every possible solution to the matching problem and find the largest one. This would be a correct algorithm. However, the number of total matchings is exponentially large in the size of the graph. Blindly writing all possible matchings down and picking the one that achieved the maximum was a “not good” algorithm. You might call it a “bad” algorithm. His new procedure was vastly more efficient.

So Edmonds spent two pages constructing a definition of good. He demanded that everyone agree on a reasonable definition for a problem size. For his matching problem, he said the size was the number of vertices plus the number of edges in the graph. A good algorithm would then have a running time upper-bounded by some well-defined function of that size, no matter how large the instance. He demanded that the running-time bound hold for every conceivable size, because he feared someone might rig the problem by planting a few small instances that were unnaturally hard.

Edmonds wasn’t completely satisfied with this definition. Indeed, he wrote:

It would be unfortunate for any rigid criterion to inhibit the practical development of algorithms which are either not known or known not to conform nicely to the criterion. Many of the best algorithmic ideas known today would suffer by such theoretical pedantry. In fact, an outstanding open question is, essentially: “how good” is a particular algorithm for linear programming, the simplex method? And, on the other hand, many important algorithmic ideas in electrical switching theory are obviously not “good” in our sense.1

With this caveat noted, he concluded his digression by announcing the complexity of his new blossom algorithm: “An upper bound on the order of difficulty of the matching algorithm is n4, where n is the number of vertices in the graph.”

Edmonds did not make any further arguments for what he meant by good. He asserted that exponential time is bad. For most algorithm designers, linear time, proportional to the input length, was naturally excellent. Moreover, our grade-school multiplication algorithm took quadratic time (multiply two three-digit numbers out by hand like you were taught in school and count the number of digits you write down when you calculate it), and that seemed pretty good. Edmonds had a matching algorithm that required a quartic number of operations. To later formalists like Richard Karp, it seemed like a “polynomial” number of operations was a reasonable definition for goodness. Polynomial time is good. Exponential time is bad. This created the field of complexity theory, with the goal of proving that all sorts of algorithms run in polynomial time and characterizing the problems for which no polynomial-time algorithm existed.

But polynomial time probably haunted Edmonds. It is not a “good” algorithm if your procedure scales like n1000, even if this is technically a polynomial. More absurdly,

is a polynomial bigger than the exponential function 2n for any n we could ever encounter. Polynomial was always an imperfect definition of good, but we ran with it. Thousands of papers later, we just have a zoo of confusing complexity results unmoored from the realities of computation.

Indeed, asymptotic thinking about how polynomials differ from exponentials enables the bad habit of designing “galactic algorithms,” conceptual procedures with running times so large they could never be implemented in our universe. I mentioned these in my earlier post about OpenAI’s Faster Fourier Transform.

This brings me back to our beneficent friends at OpenAI. This week they declared their latest breakthrough in theoretical computer science. They provided an algorithm for the satisfiability problem that ran in “subexponential time.” Satisfiability is one of the most well-known “NP complete problems, and I don’t want to go into the details of P vs NP today, but suffice it to say that you would win a Clay Millennium Prize if you could find a polynomial-time algorithm for satisfiability.2

For some unspecified constant numbers d and C. Ugly as this expression is, this was touted on Twitter as the biggest moment in theoretical computer science in 50 years. It was covered all over the tech press this week. OpenAI clearly wanted us to think it was a big fucking deal. And many theoretical computer scientists took to social media to agree.

Since it was such a big deal, I wanted to see if I could understand the algorithm a bit. Of course, as I’ve told all of you, we’re not supposed to read these papers. We’re supposed to ask ChatGPT what they say. And ChatGPT told me there was a catch.

The derived algorithm runs exhaustive search—the algorithm Edmonds declared bad in 1965—if the number of variables is less than 10^10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000.

This is a completely unfathomable number.3 There are something like 10^80 atoms in the universe. That’s 10^9,999,999,999,999,999,999,999,920 times smaller. Up until this barely finite threshold, the magic new algorithm calls an exponential-time subroutine. For any problem that we could ever consider, the procedure is exponential time. The “result” is that only in some bizarre, unknowable neighborhood of infinity, satisfiability problems are solved in subexponential time.

The claimed subexponential algorithm for satisfiability is definitive evidence that our definition of efficient was even worse than we thought it was 50 years ago. The answer tells us nothing about efficiency or goodness. Sometimes you need to answer your question to realize you wanted something else.

I’m not a betting man, but I have a prediction. It’s going to turn out that P=NP in some galactic sense, and all we’ll learn is that we spent fifty years answering the wrong question.
